newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-AZINGER THANKFUL FOR BUTTERFLIES AT MASTERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-AZINGER THANKFUL FOR BUTTERFLIES AT MASTERS.

text.p: Paul Azinger is in the hunt at the Masters Friday thanks to a return of the butterflies.

"I was a little jumpy today. You don't get the best out of yourself unless you are a little bit nervous. You don't give it your best," he said after his first-round three-under-par 69 left him two shots behind leader John Huston.
"It was just nice to have some butterflies. If you don't have those butterflies, it's probably because you don't feel like you have any chance."

Azinger, who said he did not feel the least bit nervous the last two years at Augusta National when he finished 17th and 18th, has given himself a chance at the Masters by rededicating himself to golf.
The last few years he has been preoccupied with other things in life -- natural enough after discovering late in 1993 he had cancer.

Azinger, the 1993 PGA champion, lost almost all of 1994 as he underwent treatment for lymphoma in his shoulder. He returned to competitive golf but not with the intensity of years past. Other things seemed more important.
"I wanted to live life a little bit, I guess is the bottom line," said the 36-year-old Azinger, who admitted he did not put in the practice time he once had. "I was just going through the motions."
An abysmal tournament performance changed his thinking.

"Last year at Houston, I was last by five shots and I was whining and complaining a little bit to my wife, and she said, 'Don't complain to me because you don't practice like you used to. And until you do, I don't want to hear it.'"
Azinger had done some television commentary during the Ryder Cup in 1995 and considered making a career in the booth. His agent asked him to look 10 years ahead at what he would like to be doing.
"It was a pretty deep question," Azinger said. "I realised I'm in this for the long haul."
His wife's words sank in after that Houston failure. "She was right," Azinger said. "And about then I decided to change my focus and practice a little harder."
Azinger believes his comeback from cancer is nearly complete. He has made golf a top priority once again and is seeing the results of his commitment.
"I felt starting the year that I was ready to make kind of a jump. I felt like my focus has changed a little bit."
On a breezy day Thursday when most players struggled on the difficult Augusta National layout, Azinger played solidly.

"I wasn't really sure of myself on the greens early on," he said. "I became a little more sure of myself as the day went on. But I played really well. I had a good flight on the ball, the ball spun well off my irons."
His round was set up by a brief exchange with playing partner Tom Kite, the U.S. Ryder Cup team captain he is trying to impress in hopes of being considered for this year's team.

"Tom and I were talking about the first tee shot of the day. And he made a comment, you know, 'There's not many first shots in golf that will do that to you, get your blood pumping. And that's what Augusta does.'"
Azinger agreed, and knew that meant he was back on beam and stood a chance to win another championship.
